source_text: Ὁ γὰρ τὰ κτήματα σου διατρέφων, τὴν σὴν συναύξει τοῦ βίου κατασκευήν. Ἔπειτα, ἡ τῶν σπερμάτων γένεσις τί ἄλλο ἐστὶ, καὶ οὐχὶ τῆς σῆς διαγωγῆς παρασκευή; πρὸς τῷ πολλὰ τῶν ἐν πόαις ἔτι καὶ λαχάνοις ὄντων, τροφὴν ἀνθρώπων ὑπάρχειν. 5.2 Βλαστησάτω ἡ γῆ βοτάνην χόρτου, σπεῖρον σπέρμα, φησὶ, κατὰ γένος. Ὥστε κἄν τι γένος βοτάνης ἑτέροις διαφέρῃ, κἀκείνων τὸ κέρδος πρὸς ἡμᾶς ἐπανέρχεται, καὶ ἡμῖν ἡ χρῆσις τῶν σπερμάτων ἀφώρισται· ὥστε εἶναι τὸν νοῦν τῶν εἰρημένων τοιοῦτον, Βλαστησάτω ἡ γῆ βοτάνην χόρτου, καὶ σπέρμα σπεῖρον κατὰ γένος. Οὕτω γὰρ καὶ τὸ τῆς λέξεως ἀκόλουθον ἀποκαταστῆναι δυνήσεται, ἀκαταλλήλως νῦν τῆς συντάξεως ἔχειν δοκούσης, καὶ τὸ ἀναγκαῖον τῶν ὑπὸ τῆς φύσεως οἰκονομουμένων διασωθήσεται. Πρῶτον μὲν γὰρ βλάστησις, εἶτα χλοὴ, εἶτα χόρτου αὔξησις, εἶτα ὁ ἀπαρτισμὸς τῶν αὐξομένων διὰ τοῦ σπέρματος. Πῶς οὖν, φασὶ, πάντα εἶναι τὰ ἐκ τῆς γῆς φυόμενα σπερματικὰ ὁ λόγος ἐνδείκνυται, ὅπου γε οὔτε κάλαμος, οὔτε ἄγρωστις, οὔτε ἡ μίνθη, οὐ κρόκος, οὐ σκόροδον, οὐ βούτομον, οὐδ' ἄλλα μυρία γένη φυτῶν σπερματίζοντα φαίνεται; Πρὸς δὴ τοῦτό φαμεν, ὅτι πολλὰ τῶν φυομένων ἐκ τῆς γῆς ἐπὶ τοῦ πυθμένος καὶ τῆς ῥίζης ἔχει τὴν δύναμιν τῶν σπερμάτων. Ὥσπερ ὁ κάλαμος, μετὰ τὴν ἐπέτειον αὔξησιν, ἀπὸ τῆς ῥίζης ἀφίησί τινα προβολὴν, σπέρματος λόγον ἔχουσαν, πρὸς τὸ μέλλον. Τοῦτο δὲ ποιεῖ καὶ ἄλλα μυρία, ὅσα διὰ γῆς νεμόμενα ἐν ταῖς ῥίζαις τὴν διαδοχὴν κέκτηται. Ὥστε παντός ἐστιν ἀληθέστερον τὸ, ἑκάστῳ τῶν φυομένων ἢ σπέρμα εἶναι, ἢ δύναμίν τινα σπερματικὴν ἐνυπάρχειν. Καὶ τοῦτό ἐστι τὸ, Κατὰ γένος. Οὐ γὰρ ἡ προβολὴ τοῦ καλά μου ἐλαίας ἐστὶ ποιητικὴ, ἀλλὰ ἐκ καλάμου μὲν ἕτερος κάλαμος, ἐκ δὲ τῶν σπερμάτων τὰ συγγενῆ τοῖς καταβληθεῖσιν ἀποβλαστάνει. Καὶ οὕτω τὸ ἐν τῇ πρώτῃ γενέσει προβληθὲν παρὰ τῆς γῆς, μέχρι νῦν διασώζεται, τῇ ἀκολουθίᾳ τῆς διαδοχῆς φυλασσομένου τοῦ γένους. Βλαστησάτω ἡ γῆ. Νόησόν μοι ἐκ μικρᾶς φωνῆς, καὶ προστάγματος οὕτω βραχέος, τὴν κατεψυγμένην καὶ ἄγονον ὠδίνουσαν ἀθρόως καὶ πρὸς καρπογονίαν συγκινουμένην, ὥσπερ τινὰ σκυθρωπὴν καὶ πενθήρη ἀπορρίψασαν περιβολὴν, μεταμφιεννυμένην τὴν φαιδροτέραν καὶ τοῖς οἰκείοις κόσμοις ἀγαλλομένην, καὶ τὰ μυρία γένη τῶν φυομένων προβάλλουσαν. Βούλομαί σοι σφοδρότερον τῆς κτίσεως ἐνιδρυνθῆναι τὸ θαῦμα, ἵν' ὅπου περ ἂν εὑρεθῇς, καὶ ὁποίῳ δήποτε γένει τῶν φυομένων παραστῇς, ἐναργῆ λαμβάνῃς τοῦ ποιήσαντος τὴν ὑπόμνησιν. Πρῶτον μὲν οὖν ὅταν ἴδῃς βοτάνην χόρτου καὶ ἄνθος, εἰς ἔννοιαν ἔρχου τῆς ἀνθρωπίνης φύσεως, μεμνημένος τῆς εἰκόνος τοῦ σοφοῦ Ἡσαΐου, ὅτι Πᾶσα σὰρξ ὡς χόρτος, καὶ πᾶσα δόξα ἀνθρώπου ὡς ἄνθος χόρτου. Τὸ γὰρ ὀλιγοχρόνιον τῆς ζωῆς, καὶ τὸ ἐν ὀλίγῳ περιχαρὲς καὶ ἱλαρὸν τῆς ἀνθρωπίνης εὐημερίας, καιριωτάτης παρὰ τῷ προφήτῃ τετύχηκε τῆς εἰκόνος. Σήμερον εὐθαλὴς τῷ σώματι, κατασεσαρκωμένος ὑπὸ τρυφῆς, ἐπανθοῦσαν ἔχων τὴν εὔχροιαν ὑπὸ τῆς κατὰ τὴν ἡλικίαν ἀκμῆς, σφριγῶν καὶ σύντονος, καὶ ἀνυπόστατος τὴν ὁρμὴν, αὔριον ὁ αὐτὸς οὗτος ἐλεεινὸς, ἢ τῷ χρόνῳ μαρανθεὶς, ἢ νόσῳ διαλυθείς.
orientation: Basil is explaining Genesis 1:11, arguing that every plant has seed or a seedlike power, and then turns to the moral lesson of grass and flower as an image of human frailty.
pass_a_gloss: For the one who feeds your flocks increases your own provision for life. Then, the origin of seeds—what else is it but preparation for your way of life? In addition to the fact that many of the things among grasses and vegetables are food for humans. 'Let the earth sprout the herb of grass, sowing seed,' it says, 'according to kind.' So that even if some kind of herb differs for other creatures, the benefit of those also comes back to us, and the use of the seeds is set apart for us; so that the meaning of the words is such: 'Let the earth sprout the herb of grass, and seed sowing according to kind.' For in this way the sequence of the wording will be able to be restored, since the construction now seems to be incongruous, and the necessary order of things arranged by nature will be preserved. For first is sprouting, then green growth, then increase of grass, then the completion of the growing things through the seed. How then, they say, does the account show that all things growing from the earth are seed-bearing, when neither reed, nor couch grass, nor mint, nor crocus, nor garlic, nor bulrush, nor countless other kinds of plants appear to produce seed? To this we say that many of the things growing from the earth have the power of seeds in the base and the root. Just as the reed, after its yearly growth, sends out from the root a certain shoot, having the principle of seed, for the future. And countless other things do this, as many as spread through the ground and possess succession in their roots. So that it is truer than everything that for each of the things growing there is either seed or some seedlike power existing within. And this is the meaning of 'according to kind.' For the shoot of the reed is not productive of olive, but from reed comes another reed, and from the seeds the things akin to what was cast down sprout up. And thus what was brought forth by the earth in the first generation is preserved until now, the kind being guarded by the sequence of succession. 'Let the earth sprout.' Understand for me from a small utterance and a command so brief, the frozen and barren earth suddenly in travail and stirred toward fruit-bearing, as if throwing off some gloomy and mourning garment, changing into a brighter one and rejoicing in its own ornaments, and putting forth the countless kinds of growing things. I want the wonder of creation to be fixed in you more intensely, so that wherever you may be found, and whatever kind of growing things you may stand beside, you may receive a vivid reminder of the Maker. First then, whenever you see herb of grass and flower, come to a thought of human nature, remembering the image of the wise Isaiah, that 'All flesh is as grass, and all glory of man as flower of grass.' For the short-livedness of life, and the brief joy and cheerfulness of human prosperity, has obtained from the prophet a most timely image. Today flourishing in body, fleshed out by luxury, having blooming good complexion from the prime of age, vigorous and taut, and irresistible in impulse—tomorrow this same man is pitiable, either withered by time or dissolved by disease.

choices.why: Literal rendering of the LXX phrase; keeps the genitive construction visible rather than smoothing to 'grassy herb'
λόγον here means the rational principle or formative power; 'principle of seed' preserves the philosophical sense without importing modern biology
Fixed glossary term; kept literal to show the fixed natural kinds in reproduction
Preserves the birth-pang metaphor Basil uses for the earth's sudden fertility; 'laboring' would lose the biblical resonance
ἀνυπόστατος means not to be withstood; rendering as 'irresistible' keeps the force of the adjective with the accusative of respect

pass_b_english: For the one who feeds your flocks is also building up the provision for your own life. And then, what is the origin of seeds if not a preparation for your way of living? Besides, many of the things that are still among grasses and garden herbs serve as food for human beings. "Let the earth sprout the herb of grass, sowing seed," it says, "according to kind" (Genesis 1:11). So even if some kind of herb differs from others, its benefit comes back to us, and the use of the seeds is set apart for us. The meaning of the words, then, is this: "Let the earth sprout the herb of grass, and seed sowing according to kind." In this way the sequence of the wording can be restored—since the syntax now seems inconsistent—and the necessary order of what nature arranges will be preserved. For first comes sprouting, then the green shoot, then the growth of the grass, then the completion of what grows through the seed. How then, they say, does the text show that everything growing from the earth has seed, when neither reed nor couch grass nor mint, not crocus, not garlic, not sedge, nor countless other kinds of plants appear to produce seed? To this we answer that many of the things growing from the earth have the power of their seeds in the base and the root. Just as the reed, after its yearly growth, sends out from the root a certain shoot having the principle of seed for the future. Countless other plants do the same, all that spread through the ground and possess their succession in their roots. So it is truer than anything that for each thing that grows there is either a seed or some seedlike power existing within it. And this is what "according to kind" means. For the shoot of the reed does not produce an olive tree, but from a reed comes another reed, and from seeds the things related to what was sown spring up. And so what the earth brought forth in the first creation is preserved even until now, the kind being guarded by the sequence of succession. "Let the earth sprout." Consider for me how from a small utterance and so brief a command, the frozen and barren earth suddenly travails and is stirred toward fruit-bearing, as though throwing off a gloomy and mournful garment and clothing herself in a brighter one, rejoicing in her proper ornaments and putting forth the countless kinds of growing things. I want the wonder of creation to be fixed in you more intensely, so that wherever you find yourself, and whatever kind of growing thing you stand beside, you may receive a vivid reminder of the Maker. First, then, when you see the herb of grass and a flower, bring to mind human nature, remembering the image of the wise Isaiah, that "All flesh is as grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of grass" (Isaiah 40:6). For the brevity of life, and the short-lived joy and brightness of human prosperity, has found in the prophet a most fitting image. Today a man flourishes in body, fleshed out by luxury, with his good color blooming from the prime of his age, vigorous and taut and irresistible in impulse; tomorrow this same man is pitiable, either withered by time or dissolved by disease.

last_rejected.quote: the frozen and barren earth suddenly travails
last_rejected.source_quote: τὴν κατεψυγμένην καὶ ἄγονον ὠδίνουσαν ἀθρόως καὶ πρὸς καρπογονίαν συγκινουμένην
last_rejected.why: Earth is subject of both participles: 'travails and is stirred', not 'travails' as separate verb.
last_rejected.fix: the frozen and barren earth, suddenly travailing and stirred toward fruit-bearing
last_rejected.ruling: English 'travails and is stirred' renders both participles (ὠδίνουσαν, συγκινουμένην) correctly; no meaning is lost.

last_rejected.why: κατασεσαρκωμένος means 'fattened' or 'made fleshy', not 'fleshed out' which suggests completion.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Fleshed out by luxury' reasonably renders κατασεσαρκωμένος ὑπὸ τρυφῆς; within normal range, not a major error.
